rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Organic compounds are classified into open-chain (aliphatic) and closed-chain (cyclic) compounds; cyclic compounds are homocyclic (alicyclic and aromatic) or heterocyclic."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Cyclohexane vs benzene, ring vs ring*** — both are six-membered carbon rings, but one adds hydrogen readily while the other refuses and substitutes instead: the difference is delocalised pi electrons, i.e. aromaticity.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — A Family Tree for Millions With tens of millions of organic compounds, chemistry would be impossible without classification. The tree has two great branches — **open-chain (acyclic/aliphatic)** and **closed-chain (cyclic)** — and the cyclic branch splits into **homocyclic** (alicyclic + aromatic) and **heterocyclic**. Learn the tree once and every new compound has an address.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Open-chain (acyclic / aliphatic) compounds - Chains of carbon atoms, straight or branched, **no ring**. - **Saturated (alkanes):** only single bonds — CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈. - **Unsaturated:** at least one multiple bond — **alkenes** (C=C, ethene CH₂=CH₂), **alkynes** (C≡C, ethyne HC≡CH). ### 2.2 Closed-chain (cyclic) compounds - **Homocyclic:** ring made only of carbon atoms.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Tree: open (alkane/alkene/alkyne) vs closed; closed -> homocyclic (alicyclic vs aromatic) + heterocyclic (N/O/S in ring). Aromatic = benzene-ring pi stability. Heterocyclic examples: pyridine, furan, pyrrole.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Aromatic is a stability statement: the benzene ring's delocalised pi electrons make substitution preferred over addition — that reactivity signature, not any smell, defines the aromatic branch.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Classification: open-chain (acyclic/aliphatic) — saturated alkanes (CH4, C2H6), unsaturated alkenes (C=C, ethene CH2=CH2) and alkynes (C=C triple, ethyne); closed-chain (cyclic) — homocyclic (all-carbon ring): alicyclic (cyclopropane, cyclohexane) and aromatic (benzene C6H6, toluene, naphthalene — delocalised pi…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Most drugs and natural products are heterocyclic — pyridine appears in the vitamin niacin, pyrrole rings in chlorophyll and haem, furan in the furanose form of sugars.

Common Confusions **Alicyclic ≠ aromatic:** cyclohexane's ring is just a chain bent shut — no delocalised π stability. Only the benzene-type ring is aromatic.  ·  **Heterocyclic means the ring atom, not a substituent:** ethanol has an O but it is not in a ring and is not heterocyclic; pyridine's N is in the ring — that is the criterion.
